Everything up to here was a guided tour. These are the projects where **you**
drive: pick one, run it, break it, and present what you found.

All three were chosen for the same reason — they produce an **objective metric**, not
a vibe check. "Does this sound Shakespearean?" is a matter of taste; "how many
moves before it plays something illegal?" is a number a referee computes for
you, and it either goes up or it does not.

::: {.callout-tip title="🎯 What makes a good presentation"}
Not "we ran the code and it worked." The interesting talks are the ones with a
**comparison** and a **surprise**:

1. A plot with your metric on the y-axis and training step on the x-axis.
2. Two curves on that plot, differing by *one* decision you made.
3. An honest account of what you expected and what actually happened.

All three starters below already contain a built-in surprise. Reproduce it first,
then go find your own.
:::

## The three starters

- 🏆 **[\[5.0\] Chess GPT](./0-chess-gpt/)** — train the
  [\[2.3\]](../02-llms/3-shakespeare-ezpz/) model from scratch on real
  tournament games. The metric is *legal moves before a blunder*, and the
  built-in surprise is that the tokenization with the **lower loss** plays
  **much worse chess**.

- 🧮 **[\[5.1\] Arithmetic by RL](./1-arithmetic-grpo/)** — the
  [\[3.4\]](../03-advanced-llms/4-rl-and-reasoning/) GRPO recipe where the entire
  reward is a one-line Python check. The built-in surprise is **diversity
  collapse**: the policy learns to give the *same* answer to every question, and one extra
  term brings it back.

- 🗣️ **[\[5.2\] Fine-tuning on slang](./2-slang-finetune/)** — the other two train
  from scratch; this one fine-tunes a **real pretrained open model** (`SmolLM2`)
  on a [Gen Z slang dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MLBtrio/genz-slang-dataset).
  The built-in surprise is that the **held-out loss and the task metric peak at
  different epochs** — early-stopping on loss, which is what everyone does,
  picks the wrong checkpoint.

All three run in a few minutes on a laptop CPU, and all three scale to many GPUs
with `ezpz launch` and no code changes.

## Getting the code

The scripts live in the repo under `capstone/`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/saforem2/intro-hpc-bootcamp
cd intro-hpc-bootcamp
python3 capstone/chess_gpt.py --help
python3 capstone/arithmetic_grpo.py --help
```

On Perlmutter, everything is already installed in the shared environment — see
the [running instructions](../#running-instructions).

## Other directions

If neither of these grabs you, the same "train from scratch on a weird corpus,
then measure something objective" shape works for a lot of data:

| corpus | the metric that makes it a project |
|:--|:--|
| **SMILES molecules** (ChEMBL/ZINC) | % of generated strings that RDKit says are valid molecules |
| **Protein sequences** (UniProt) | amino-acid composition vs. real proteins |
| **ArXiv abstracts** in one field | perplexity on held-out abstracts from the same vs. a different field |
| **Sheet music** (ABC notation) | % that parse as valid music; do the key signatures stay consistent? |

The pattern is always the same: swap the corpus, keep the model, and find a
**verifier** — a piece of code that scores the output without you in the loop.
That is the single most transferable idea in this bootcamp.
